content: Blurred vision can manifest as either unilateral or bilateral. Historical Perspective There is limited information available regarding the historical context of blurred vision. Classification There is no universally established system for classifying blurred vision. Pathophysiology Blurred vision may arise from refractive errors, opacities in ocular structures such as the lens, cornea, or vitreous, retinal disorders, or diseases affecting the optic nerve. By the age of 65, approximately one in three individuals experiences some form of vision-reducing eye disorder. Risk Factors Risk factors contributing to the development of blurred vision include genetic predisposition, nutritional deficiencies, family history, diabetes mellitus, advancing age, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, exposure to toxins, and ultraviolet light exposure. Screening According to the American Diabetes Association, patients with type 1 diabetes should undergo a comprehensive eye examination within five years of diabetes onset, while those with type 2 diabetes should have an eye exam at the time of diagnosis. Annual follow-up examinations are recommended thereafter. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine glaucoma screening. However, the USPSTF advises that individuals at increased risk, particularly African Americans and older adults, consult their primary care clinician or eye care specialist for guidance on glaucoma screening. The USPSTF recommends annual blood pressure screening for adults aged 40 years or older and for those at increased risk of hypertension. High-risk individuals include those with high-normal blood pressure (130–139/85–89 mmHg), overweight or obese individuals, and African Americans. Adults aged 18 to 39 years with normal blood pressure (<130/85 mmHg) and no other risk factors should be re-screened every 3 to 5 years. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis The prognosis of blurred vision depends on the underlying cause. Diagnosis There are no established diagnostic criteria for blurred vision. Patients should be asked about the onset, duration, associated symptoms, and whether the blurred vision is unilateral or bilateral. History and Symptoms Common symptoms accompanying blurred vision include eye redness, eye pain, excessive tearing (epiphora), headache, light sensitivity (photophobia), halos, nausea, excessive thirst (polydipsia), excessive urination (polyuria), dizziness, and numbness. Physical Examination An eye examination for patients with blurred vision should include: Visual acuity testing Visual field examination Slit lamp examination Ophthalmoscopy Tonometry Angle testing (gonioscopy) The presence of sudden hemiplegia, abnormal gait, ataxia, and dysarthria is diagnostic of cerebrovascular accident. Laboratory Findings Patients with systemic disorders should undergo appropriate testing. Elevated blood sugar and hemoglobin A1C levels are indicative of blurred vision caused by diabetes mellitus. Urinalysis and renal function tests should be considered in patients with hypertension. Antinuclear antibodies and elevated ESR are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and vasculitis. A complete blood count (CBC) with differential and other tests may be necessary in cases of leukemia or multiple myeloma. Imaging A CT scan of the brain may help diagnose mass-occupying lesions or ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. MRI of the brain and orbits can confirm optic nerve inflammation. Treatment Treatment depends on the underlying cause, and associated disorders should be addressed. Patients with refractive errors and presbyopia can be treated with corrective lenses or eyeglasses. Supportive therapy for hyphema includes elevating the head of the bed, wearing an eye shield, and reducing physical activity. Patients with wet macular degeneration may benefit from anti-VEGF medications or photodynamic therapy to inhibit the growth of new blood vessels. Medical Therapy Diabetic retinopathy can be treated with direct injections or intravitreal administration of anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenesis agents (e.g., anti-VEGF drugs), which are effective for diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema. Laser treatment is an option for diabetic retinopathy. Pharmacologic therapy with eye drops is recommended for glaucoma patients. Infectious cases are treated with antibacterial, antiviral, or antiparasitic agents. Corticosteroids are used to treat uveitis, iritis, and optic neuritis. High-dose corticosteroids are the treatment of choice for temporal arteritis. Hypertension is managed with antihypertensive medications. Surgery LASIK surgery is commonly used to correct refractive errors. Surgical interventions for presbyopia are still under study. Surgery is the primary treatment for cataracts and retinal detachment. Vitrectomy is used to treat diabetic retinopathy. Glaucoma surgeries include trabeculoplasty, iridotomy, and trabeculectomy. Primary Prevention Preventive measures for diabetic retinopathy include maintaining a healthy lifestyle, controlling hypertension, stringent lipid control, and periodic ophthalmic examinations. Smoking cessation is strongly encouraged, as studies confirm an increased risk of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) among smokers. Secondary Prevention Early detection and treatment of refractive errors in school vision programs are effective measures for preventing blurred vision due to refractive errors. Secondary prevention of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease includes lifestyle interventions, weight management, antihypertensive agents, statin therapy, antiplatelet therapy, diabetes management, and smoking cessation.
